articles.title: My uncle is a ghost
articles.description: In the distance, outside the window of the bedroom I grew up in, rises a tall, narrow, sleek corporate Gothic-style tower with columns of vertical windows and a grey-silver carapace. Its design, base and architect (Minoru Yamasaki) match New York's World Trade Center twin towers, just half the height. On the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, I found myself thinking about the view outside my window. The specter of 9/11 has hung over my entire life. I was born in 2005, still during the ramp-up of the War on Terror. My sister was born two months after the towers fell. On the morning of 9/11, my uncle was in the North Tower when it collapsed. The death of my uncle has always been a tricky subject to broach. Because of that, how I have processed this family tragedy - and the broader implications of the attacks of 9/11 - has always been fragmented. It has impacted all of us in our own ways. When I don't know what to think, I write. For this subject, I feel I can do neither. My uncle is a ghost. I've tried to piece together his final days. They haunt me. The week of Sept. 4, he was on vacation with his siblings, parents and my mother. In the photos, he's vivid, full of life. He jokes about life insurance at 25 for his new job. On Sept. 8 or 9, he goes back to New York early for work. That morning, he heads to the 106th floor of the North Tower for a business meeting. Finally, he feels the impact, coughs on the smoke, and emails his sister goodbye. 부모가 죽으면 산에 묻고 자식이 죽으면 가슴에 묻는다. It's a Korean proverb. When a parent dies, they are buried in the ground; when a child dies, they are buried in the heart. They never found his body. I did not know Peter; I cannot tell you how funny, popular, quirky or anything he was. But I feel him. I feel his ghost. In his images I see my father, I see myself, and I see the darkness where he is buried in my father's heart. I wonder how much of him could be buried in mine. The terror attacks of 9/11 stole from me an uncle. A man I've come to know through disparate photographs, memorabilia and stories, all now mired in a heavy layer of both nostalgia and grief. My mother would tell me stories about him, his hobbies, his sense of humor; apparently, I would have gotten along with him. My father speaks less of his late brother. Though I never met Peter, I do feel a deep sense of grief for the relationship lost. It's a difficult pain to express, a deep sense of loss for someone you never knew, but whose loss has marked my family deeply, and which now burdens me. I've seen in my family how grief can transform people and relationships. Grief doesn't simply dissipate. It moves sideways; it permeates into silence, into anger, into someone else. It can hurt. It can be passed on, but it does not go away. This pain now exists within me. A deep-seated sense of injustice, a feeling from before my birth that my family was once whole and is not now, grips us as we are now by the ghost of my uncle. Things didn't just change on 9/11; on that day, a part of our family was taken, and a piece of all of us died with his murder. My family will forever be defined in some part by that loss. It has been a difficult family dynamic to reckon with. In 1953, U.S.-backed forces in Iran launched a bloody coup d'état against Iran's Mossadegh to install the Shah and ensure Iranian oil belonged to the West. After the Gulf War, the U.S. maintained a significant military presence in Saudi Arabia to secure oil fields. Globally, America inspired fear, anger and grief. None of this is a justification for 9/11. Yet in the ensuing days, America as a country was consumed by grief. Nearly 3,000 innocents were suddenly murdered in the largest city in the most powerful country in the world. The U.S. War on Terror was an unmitigated disaster. Brown University's Costs of War Project has published that U.S. action in Syria, Yemen, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Iraq and beyond killed 4.5 million people, with roughly half of those killed civilians. From those regions, 38 million more were displaced. After 20 years, 4 presidents and $7 trillion, America packed up and went home. It did not achieve its objectives. These numbers are hard to grasp; more so is the suffering American action in the Middle East brought about. A single death is a tragedy; a million deaths are a statistic. My uncle is a statistic. One drop in the bucket of a forever war from which nobody reigns victorious. His death scars me, wounds me, leaves me searching for answers where there are none. And to see his killing co-opted, warped, twisted into a cry for hate hurts even more. He is a victim of xenophobia, hatred and malice. But he is also a victim of American greed and exceptionalism. On 9/11, America reaped what it had sown for decades. In the wake of the attacks, that sense of loss was leveraged, compounded. Our leadership beat the drums for war, choosing revenge instead of healing, offense as defense; we ourselves chose terror. That isolated and swept terror inward. America endured as we had endured, and as we were directed to endure: bravado and bluster, anger and vitriol. They say evil prevails when good men fail to act. They should say evil prevails. I wonder how many others feel a pull, feel a specter hang over their family. I think about the others who lost children, brothers, mothers on that day. I think about those flag-draped coffins of boys dead in the Middle East, buried in American hearts. I think about ruined houses in Kandahar province, those killed by a drone because of metadata and buried in Afghan hearts. None of these bring Peter back; none of them help me bury him deeper. I do not grieve righteously. I feel a grim satisfaction at Osama Bin Laden's death. But still, the ghost follows me. I cannot find it within me to forgive America, or the terrorists. But I can say we fucked up. We propagated violence. We created millions of ghosts and so much hatred. And it brought nobody back, brought no peace. I do not have a message. I am conflicted, haunted, unresolved. And I am reminded of that by something as little as looking out the window. Sebastian Alderman (they/them) is a senior from Tulsa, Okla., studying Anthropology and History on the pre-med track.

articles.title: Scifi Magazine 'Starlog' Relaunches, and Back Issues Return to Internet Archive
articles.description: Slashdot reader sandbagger brings news about the classic science ficdtion magazine Starlog. It's 33-year run from 1976 to 2009 is now available on the Internet Archive. And 17 years after publishing its final issue, Starlog is relaunching, publishing one issue a year starting November 13, according to The Hollywood Reporter: The magazine launched in 1976 and gained a fanbase for being one of the few places to get reliable news and interviews about geek culture. It launched with a cover focusing on Star Trek, one of its key areas of expertise, but the magazine's editors and writers also pioneered coverage of Star Wars. (The new issue chronicles some of the rumors it put out a year before the movie opened). In all, Starlog published 374 issues and more than 25,000 pages... In addition to the film and TV-focused features Starlog was known for, the new Starlog will also delve into futurism, as the cover from Gabriel Yeganyan highlights. The opening story of issue No. 1 looks at the viability of humans farming crops on planets outside of Earth, for example... The revival was announced earlier this year, and includes a podcast hosted by Jordan Hoffman, a veteran journalist who has contributed to The Hollywood Reporter. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Cardi BRB: the worst "concert" I've been to
articles.description: The way I saw it, the Cardi B concert was pretty lame. Key words: The way I saw it. Yes, I am a bandwagoner. I didn't know anything about Cardi B before the 2026 Hoptoberfest concert. She replaced Daniel Caesar, someone I didn't (and still don't) know, which is why I didn't bother getting a ticket in the first place. So, scrambling, I did what any industrious bandwagoner-in-the-making would have done: I inquired about obtaining a The News-Letter press pass in order to cover the concert. It was, then, under my journalistic auspices that, on the night of Halloween, my Cardi B-fanatic friend and I learned the WAP in his house. That way, no one could accuse me of uninformed coverage. Of course, I'm being facetious. One experience is all it takes to write a review of something. I could have gone into the concert blindfolded, and if I had a ticket and the brain to write an article, you'd be reading a bonafide review. But if I didn't have a ticket, then is what you're reading right now really a review? Is it really a review if my experience was so far removed - literally - from everyone else's as to be an unrecognizable species of what was supposed to be the same viewing? As its writer, let me tell you: No, it's not. Let me explain. I'm not in the business of the politics behind what student organization at Hopkins does what. I cannot correctly identify every word in the acronyms for HOP and LEED, which I understand to be behind this concert, though I do not understand their division of labor. The lede of this article, on the same concert, can tell you some of this, or at least enlighten you as to the acronyms. The long and short of it is this: When I tried presenting my press pass, it did not work. Everyone I interacted with was nice enough, and I sympathize with the struggle of managing an A-list celebrity's concert at a college campus. But in the end, I was relegated to the track above all the ground-floor action, looking down on the Halloweekend fun like Rapunzel trapped in her castle. While my friend moshed alone in a sea of strangers, I stood respectfully among most of whom I assumed to be event staff and organizers - including an old white man in a smart blue button-up drinking a Celsius, looking as confused as I was. To be honest, and without sounding sore, it was a Halloweekend of FOMO. I didn't do nothing: With my friends, we engaged in wholesome activities, like going to Weber's Farm one day and passing out candy to children in costumes on Halloween night. But like any good college student, I yearned for a more raucous fun. The Hoptoberfest concert, to the extent that any event on Hopkins' campus could, was supposed to deliver. Instead, it was merely a capstone to a Halloweekend spent as if separated from peers my age by glass. I am prone to overanalysis. That's why I was looking forward to the concert getting underway, so I could stand and maybe sway for a few songs, alone, before I could slip out unnoticed. But hours of standing, from the line to inside, begot hours of standing - and, for me, nothing really happening. I kept a Quick Note open in my phone, titled "cardi article notes" with leagues of observations that won't see light. It was only a way to make myself appear as if I had anything to do. If you're noticing how this "review" on the Cardi concert involves shockingly little of Cardi, then I've done a good job: That's exactly how the concert felt. After originally being scheduled for 7 p.m., then pushed back to take place from 7:45-9:45 p.m., Cardi B made her way on stage at the ripe time of 10:30 p.m., totaling a grand performance time of 23 minutes thereafter. In a group chat with my friends - just another one of my refuges from seeming as if I was standing alone - one texted, "cardi Brb." The music was what I expected, which was nothing, because I was unfamiliar with her music. I enjoyed the performance. Although, those 23 minutes felt more like staying to prove a point than out of earnest excitement. I may be alone in this regard because, as I was walking out, I heard someone say, "Honestly? Worth the wait." I didn't agree, but then again, of course I wouldn't. Cardi B's music was not why I wanted to attend the concert. Cardi was great; the concert was not. A concert is an experience. It isn't a person, nor is it a curated selection of that person's music. Unlike a particular poem or specific song, a concert does not have a stable identity or set content. It's a noun, empty without a modifier. Something waiting to be filled. So a "concert review," in my opinion, is not one's thoughts on the artist or if they do or don't like the music. It's a chronicling of the experience of witnessing something live. In a concert review, tantamount to the artist's performance is the weather outside, what it felt like waiting in line, whether a man danced too close to you or not or whether your shoes never smelled the same after because someone spilled a drink on them. I waited almost an hour outside. I was pulled out of the line, then sent on a wild goose chase of who to see to be allowed to stay, then kenneled above with a nice view and only a phone to share it with. I waited and stood for more hours. During "Party in the U.S.A.," I watched arms wave like sea anemone. I played the stick in the mud to an audience of one: myself. Cardi came, she left. Cardi BRB. At least now I know how to WAP. I came, I went. No one conquered. It's the one concert I've managed to go to where I felt worse leaving than entering. The prospect of a night spent in, doing homework instead, thrilled me. Concert review? It was shit.

articles.title: These Solar Panels Stay Cool in Hot Climates
articles.description: Summer heat is a major problem for silicon solar panels. They typically lose 0.5 percent of their efficiency for every degree their temperature rises above 25 °C. That’s a problem in hot places like Baghdad, where air temperatures can top 50 °C and prolonged sunlight can push panel surfaces toward 80 °C. In those kinds of extreme conditions, solar panel efficiency has been shown to drop by as much as 25 percent. But new research out of Iraq could provide a cooling solution that boosts solar panel efficiency in hot and sunny conditions. The system uses a water-soaked pad behind the solar panel to provide evaporative cooling, and intermittent water spraying across its front surface to prevent overheating. This strategy can improve electrical efficiency by about 20 percent, the researchers reported in late September in Results in Engineering. The system also generated cooler air that could potentially be used for building ventilation. Existing solar panel cooling methods, such as fan-assisted cooling and passive ventilation, can struggle to adequately regulate temperatures under extreme heat, says Deyaa M. N. Mahmood, a thermal power systems expert at Middle Technical University in Baghdad and lead author of the paper. But Baghdad’s extremely dry air offers an opportunity to use a different approach. Its low relative humidity of around 15–20 percent, Mahmood says, “provides the ideal thermodynamic environment for highly efficient latent evaporative cooling.” How Does Solar Panel Cooling Work? Mahmood and his team’s strategy involves adding water-spraying nozzles, an evaporative cooling pad, and a temperature sensor to a photovoltaic module. The evaporative pad, made of cellulose, covers the back of the solar panel and a perforated tube distributes water evenly across it. Meanwhile, a fan draws ambient air through the pad, causing evaporation and cooling the module. When the panel’s front surface reaches 42–45 °C, nozzles automatically spray water across it to reduce surface heat and remove dust. A collection tank recovers runoff water from both the rear pad and front spray so it can be recirculated, reducing the amount of fresh water needed. In the best-performing configuration with a 100-millimeter-thick pad, the panel’s temperature dropped by 29.7 °C relative to an uncooled panel. Electrical conversion efficiency also improved by about 20 percent. The researchers tested the system in July, August, and September, collecting measurements during Baghdad’s hottest and sunniest hours. The team arrived at this design after building previous prototypes, one of which used a groundwater-to-air heat exchanger to pre-cool incoming air before reaching the pad. That design, however, added practical limitations by relying on deep-well infrastructure and substantial pumping power. The latest prototype combines evaporative cooling behind the panel with intermittent water spraying on the front, activating only when needed. This allows the system to cool both sides and wash away dust without relying on energy-intensive groundwater systems. “Combining these two methods addresses the core limitations of standalone systems,” Mahmood says. Rear-only evaporative cooling can become less effective when ambient air temperatures exceed 50 °C. Solar Panel Efficiency Drops in Hot Climates A key engineering challenge in the new design involved adapting the evaporative cellulose pad to the test rig’s 33° incline—the optimal fixed-tilt angle for solar panels in Baghdad’s latitude. Such pads are typically installed vertically in evaporative air coolers and greenhouse ventilation systems, allowing water to flow evenly downward via gravity. Installing the pad at an angle required adjustments to water flow and distribution to prevent dry spots or water channeling, Mahmood says. Reducing the temperature of the panel by nearly 30 °C in extreme conditions is impressive, say Qiaoqiang Gan and Sunmiao Fang, materials science researchers at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) who were not involved in the research. Previous water-spray cooling efforts reported temperature reductions of about 10 °C to 22 °C and electrical efficiency improvements of roughly 7 to 24 percent, according to a study published in May in Scientific Reports. But comparisons between cooling technologies should account for many factors. “The reported cooling performance is encouraging, but the ultimate value of PV cooling technologies should be evaluated based on their net energy benefits, water consumption, and long-term operating costs, rather than temperature reduction alone,” says Gan, a professor at KAUST. Energy and Water Trade-Offs in PV Cooling In Mahmood’s system, the best-performing configuration increased the average electrical output of a 150-watt PV module by approximately 16.7 W. However, the system used a fan and pumps for water circulation and spraying, potentially impacting those gains. Actual power consumption and operating cycles must be considered when evaluating net electrical benefits, says Fang, a postdoctoral researcher at KAUST. Mahmood acknowledges the shortcoming. “In our single-panel prototype setup, the parasitic energy consumed by the pump and fan actually exceeded the immediate electrical power gain generated by the cooling effect, a well-known limitation inherent to small-scale prototypes,” he says. This could be mitigated somewhat in full-scale commercial installations, where shared pumping and fan infrastructure can scale across a large array, reducing overhead per panel. Mahmood also sees potential energy savings from integrating the system with building ventilation. “What surprised us most was the exceptional thermal quality of the rear exhaust air,” Mahmood says. After passing through the water-soaked cellulose pad, the cooled air could be directed to pre-cool Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) fresh-air intake units. “When accounting for the secondary thermal energy saved by using the cooled exhaust air for building HVAC pre-cooling, the total net energy balance of the system becomes highly favorable,” Mahmood says. Solar Panel Cooling Can Also Cool Buildings How well the system could cool buildings remains unverified. The researchers reported an outlet air temperature of around 34 °C, which would require further cooling for indoor comfort, notes Fang. Other deployment considerations in arid regions include water availability, dust buildup, mineral deposits, nozzle clogs, and maintenance. The reliance on powered fans and pumps could also complicate installations in areas with unreliable electricity. Fang says the technology may suit buildings with reliable water and existing ventilation, but installation, retrofitting, electricity, and maintenance costs could offset savings in small residential or off-grid systems. Mahmood’s team at Middle Technical University is seeking solar project developers and HVAC manufacturing partners for a full-scale commercial pilot.
